client: I've been completely overwhelmed thinking about my final exams next month, especially statistics. No matter how much I study, I just freeze up during practice tests and feel like I'm not making any progress. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help when I know I just need to study more.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling stuck and discouraged, even though you're putting in a lot of effort. When you think about the exams, what specific thoughts come up that make you feel like you're not making progress?

client: I keep thinking "I'm never going to understand this material" and "I'll definitely fail the exam." Even when I get some practice questions right, I focus on the ones I got wrong and feel like I'm not improving at all. It's like my brain just shuts down when I see the test paper in front of me.
therapist: It seems like those negative thoughts are really taking over, especially when you focus on what went wrong instead of what went right. What would it feel like to notice and acknowledge even small improvements as you study?

client: I guess it would feel better to focus on small wins, but part of me thinks "What's the point if I'm still getting things wrong?" It feels like unless I understand everything perfectly, I'm still going to fail. The anxiety just makes it hard to believe any progress is meaningful.
therapist: It sounds like the fear of not being perfect is really overshadowing your efforts, even when you're making some progress. What do you think it would take to feel like "good enough" is still a step in the right direction?

client: Honestly, I don't know if I could ever feel that way. In my program, anything less than 90% might as well be failing because of how competitive grad school applications are. When I think about "good enough," it just makes me more anxious because I know it won't actually be enough.
therapist: It sounds like the pressure you're feeling goes beyond just the exams—it's tied to bigger life goals, which makes it feel even heavier. What would it be like to separate the idea of "good enough" for this exam from the broader pressures of grad school applications?

client: I guess I could try to separate them, but it feels impossible. Every exam feels like it’s directly tied to my future, and if I don’t do well, I’ll ruin my chances of getting into grad school. It’s hard to see this as just one test when it feels like everything depends on it.
therapist: It sounds like this exam feels like it’s carrying the weight of your entire future, which must feel incredibly heavy. What would it be like to focus just on preparing for this one test, rather than letting it represent everything about your grad school dreams?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to separate them when my professors keep talking about how our grades in these core classes will make or break our applications. Maybe if I wasn't in such a competitive program it would be easier, but every class feels like it's setting me up for success or failure in grad school.
therapist: It sounds like the pressure isn't just coming from within—your professors' messages are reinforcing this all-or-nothing mindset. How does it feel when you notice how much their words are influencing your anxiety about these exams?

client: It feels frustrating because I know they’re just trying to motivate us, but it’s making everything worse. I already put so much pressure on myself, and hearing them say things like "this exam will determine your future" just makes me feel like I’m doomed if I don’t get it perfect. I wish I could tune it out, but it’s hard when it feels like they’re reminding us every class.
therapist: It sounds like their words are adding an extra layer of pressure that’s already overwhelming for you. What would it feel like to remind yourself that their messages are about motivating the group, not predicting your individual future?

client: I never really thought about it that way before. I guess it makes sense that they're speaking to the whole class, but it still feels personal when I'm the one struggling. Even if they don't mean it as a prediction, their words make me feel like the stakes are so high that one bad exam could ruin everything.
therapist: It sounds like those messages are landing in a way that feels deeply personal, even if that wasn’t the intention. When you think about the stakes, what would it be like to remind yourself that one exam doesn’t define your entire potential for grad school?

client: I know logically that one exam shouldn't define everything, but it's hard to believe it when I'm surrounded by classmates who seem to have perfect grades. I keep thinking about how admissions committees will compare my transcript to theirs, and that's what makes this feel so life-or-death. The rational part of me knows you're right, but the anxious part screams louder.
therapist: It sounds like the comparison to your classmates is really amplifying the pressure, even though you know logically that one exam doesn’t define everything. What would it feel like to focus on your own progress and strengths, rather than measuring yourself against others?

client: I wish I could focus just on my own progress, but it's hard when we all share study spaces and people casually talk about their practice test scores. Even when I try not to compare, someone will say they got a 95% and I'll spiral because I got a 75%. It makes me feel like I'm already falling behind.
therapist: It sounds like these comparisons are really triggering for you, even when you try to avoid them. What would it look like to create a study plan that focuses on your own growth, rather than reacting to others' scores?
